query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance to corrosion of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications can be explained by the formation of a stable passivation film enriched with Cr, which acts as a barrier to prevent the dissolution of the underlying metal into the corrosive environment.
generation.material_initial_state: Steels with high Cr content, such as stainless steels and high-entropy alloys
generation.intervention: Exposure to corrosive environments, such as molten salts or aqueous solutions
generation.conditions: High temperatures, presence of moisture or impurities in the corrosive environment
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a passivation film enriched with Cr
generation.mechanism: Selective dissolution of Fe and oxidation of Cr, leading to the formation of a stable passivation film
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance of steels with high Cr content, such as stainless steels and high-entropy alloys
generation.baseline: Corrosion resistance of steels without high Cr content
generation.boundary: Limited to steels with high Cr content, and corrosive environments with high temperatures and presence of moisture or impurities
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of passivation film formation and its stability in different corrosive environments is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Exposure of steels with high Cr content to corrosive environments with varying temperatures and presence of moisture or impurities
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the corrosion rate of steels with high Cr content is not significantly lower than that of steels without high Cr content, or if the passivation film composition and thickness do not correlate with the corrosion resistance, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
